title: Geometric nodal-fibre criterion for smooth double-branch pinching
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme], let $X\to S$ be proper, flat and finitely presented [def-weil-proper-morphism, def-weil-flat-morphism, def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation], and let $Z,T$ be finite etale $S$-schemes [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism, def-weil-etale-morphism]. Let $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be a closed immersion into the relative smooth locus [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], and let $j:Z\to T$ be finite etale of constant degree two [def-pc-finite-locally-free]. Let $P\to S$ be a proper finitely presented scheme with compatible $S$-maps $a:X\to P$, $b:T\to P$. Suppose that for every geometric point $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S$, where $\Omega$ is algebraically closed, the square with vertices $Z_\Omega,X_\Omega,T_\Omega,P_\Omega$ is a scheme pushout [def-weil-geometric-fibre, def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. Assume that every $X_\Omega$ is nonempty, reduced of pure dimension one [def-pc-reduced-scheme, def-weil-pure-dimension], and that every nonsmooth closed point $x\in X_\Omega$ satisfies $\widehat{\mathcal O}_{X_\Omega,x}\cong\Omega[[u,v]]/(uv)$ [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion, def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Then every $P_\Omega$ is nonempty, reduced of pure dimension one and has the same completed-local-ring condition at its nonsmooth closed points. Each nonclosed point of either geometric curve is smooth. The schemes $Z_\Omega,T_\Omega$ are finite disjoint unions of $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$, and over each $t\in T_\Omega$ there are two distinct smooth branch points $z_1,z_2\in X_\Omega$. The maps identify $X_\Omega\setminus Z_\Omega$ with $P_\Omega\setminus T_\Omega$, preserving the old singularities there, and at $b_\Omega(t)$ one has $$\widehat{\mathcal O}_{P_\Omega,b_\Omega(t)}\cong\Omega[[u]]\times_\Omega\Omega[[v]]\cong\Omega[[u,v]]/(uv).$$ Fibres and base schemes need not be connected, the two branches may belong to the same irreducible component, and $Z=T=\varnothing$ is permitted. No flatness of $P/S$, projective embedding, trait hypothesis, or splitting of $Z,T$ over $S$ is assumed.

proof.text: Fix a geometric point $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S$ and abbreviate its fibres by $C=X_\Omega$, $E=Z_\Omega$, $F=T_\Omega$, $Q=P_\Omega$. Properness and finite presentation pass to $C,Q$. Finiteness and etaleness pass to $E,F$ and to $j_\Omega:E\to F$, and the base-changed $i$ is a closed immersion. A smooth open of $X/S$ containing $Z$ pulls back to a smooth open of $C/\Omega$ containing $E$. These are arbitrary base changes; no flatness of $P/S$ or of the geometric point is used.

The finite $\Omega$-schemes $E,F$ are affine. Apply the etale-algebra decomposition to their rings and then the spectrum-of-a-product node. Every finite extension of the algebraically closed field $\Omega$ is $\Omega$: the minimal polynomial of each element splits and, being irreducible, is linear. Thus $E,F$ are finite disjoint unions of $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$. For each $t\in F$, fibre degree is preserved under base change from $j:Z\to T$, so the fibre of $j_\Omega$ over $t$ has degree two. Its etale algebra is $\Omega^r$; its vector-space dimension is $r$, hence $r=2$. Consequently $j_\Omega$ is surjective with exactly two distinct points over every $t$. The closed immersion into $C$ keeps these points distinct, closed and smooth.

The proper finite-type $\Omega$-scheme $C$ is Noetherian, so has finitely many irreducible components. Pure dimension one implies $\dim C\leq1$: an irreducible closed subset lies in a component, and a chain stays in that component. The reduced-curve-normalization node therefore supplies a dense open $U\subset C$ isomorphic to an open in a smooth $\Omega$-scheme, so $U$ is smooth. Here is the elementary topological conversion needed for nonclosed points. If a nonclosed point $x$ were not generic in a component $D$ containing it, a strict specialization $y$ of $x$ would give the chain $\overline{\{y\}}\subsetneq\overline{\{x\}}\subsetneq D$, contradicting $\dim D=1$. Every component generic point lies in $U$: otherwise the closed complement would contain that component and contain its nonempty open part outside the other finitely many components, contradicting density. Thus every nonclosed point of $C$ is smooth.

source.place: Tags 0BXR (lemma-normalization-locally-algebraic), 0B8Y (lemma-regular-point-on-curve), as used in etale-cohomology.tex Tag 0A3Q (lemma-somewhat-easier); the dimension-chain conversion is written here.

proof.text: The pair $(C,\varnothing)$ is a semistable multipointed $\Omega$-curve in the precise sense required by the field pinching theorem. Its structure morphism is flat by the field-flatness node and finitely presented by step 1; its only scheme-theoretic fibre has pure dimension one. The empty marking is flat, finitely presented, etale and of pure dimension zero vacuously. Every point of $C$ is smooth or an ordinary double point: step 3 treats the nonclosed points and the hypothesis treats the remaining nonsmooth closed points. For the chosen algebraic geometric fibre in the semistability definition, an algebraic closure of the already algebraically closed $\Omega$ is isomorphic to $\Omega$ (every algebraic element has linear minimal polynomial). Thus this pointwise verification is exactly its geometric-fibre condition, including the stated completed-local-ring definition of an ordinary double point.

source.place: Tag 0E36 (lemma-complete-local-ring-pushout), hypotheses checked against the multipointed-curve definitions; conversion from the chosen algebraic closure is explicit.

proof.text: Apply the field pinching theorem with $k=\Omega$, reference scheme $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$, $X=C$, $E=E$, $F=F$, and reference maps their structure maps. Properness, semistability, finite split branch schemes, the smooth closed immersion and surjectivity with two-point fibres were verified in steps 1--4. It supplies a pushout $Y$, a finite surjection $v:C\to Y$, a closed immersion $F\to Y$, the cartesian square, a complement isomorphism, pure dimension one from semistability, and at each $t\in F$ the isomorphisms $\widehat{\mathcal O}_{Y,t}\cong\Omega[[u]]\times_\Omega\Omega[[v]]\cong\Omega[[u,v]]/(uv)$. Both $Y$ and the given $Q$ are pushouts in all schemes. The universal property gives inverse isomorphisms $Y\simeq Q$ commuting with both maps; their composites are identities since they restrict to identities on $C$ and $F$. Hence all these assertions hold for the specified maps to $Q$.

For reducedness use the Ferrand structure-sheaf formula, verifying its extra affine-neighbourhood hypothesis first. For $t\in F$ choose an affine open $W\subset Q$ containing $b(t)$. Since $v:C\to Q$ is finite, $v^{-1}W$ is affine and contains the two points above $t$; the cartesian square in step 5 identifies these with $i(j_\Omega^{-1}(t))$. The map $j_\Omega$ is integral, being finite. Thus the Ferrand node applies to this same diagram, and uniqueness of the pushout gives its formula on $Q$. On its simultaneous affine charts the ring is $A\times_D B\subset A\times B$, where $A$ is the ring of an open in the reduced $C$, and $B$ is the ring of an open in $F$, hence a finite product of fields. Both are reduced. A nilpotent pair has zero first and second coordinate, so the subring is reduced. The affine charts cover $Q$, proving reducedness in the scheme definition.

source.place: Tag 0E25 (proposition-pushout-along-closed-immersion-and-integral), fibre-product structure sheaf and simultaneous affine charts.

proof.text: Surjectivity of $C\to Q$ and nonemptiness of $C$ imply nonemptiness of $Q$. Pure dimension one was supplied in step 5 and reducedness in step 6. Now $Q$ is proper, hence separated and of finite type, over $\Omega$ (step 1), reduced and of pure dimension one, so the argument of step 3 applies verbatim to $Q$: it is Noetherian with finitely many components, has $\dim Q\le1$, the reduced-curve-normalization node gives a dense smooth open, and every nonclosed point of $Q$ is a component generic point lying in it, hence smooth. Let $q\in Q$ be a nonsmooth closed point. If $q\in F$, its completed ring is the one calculated in step 5. Otherwise the complement isomorphism $C\setminus E\simeq Q\setminus F$ over $\Omega$ identifies local rings, smoothness and completions, so the corresponding point $c\in C$ is nonsmooth; by step 3 it is therefore closed in $C$, and the hypothesis gives $\widehat{\mathcal O}_{Q,q}\cong\widehat{\mathcal O}_{C,c}\cong\Omega[[u,v]]/(uv)$. The argument uses no connectedness or condition on which component contains each branch. If $F$ is empty, then $E$ is empty, the pushout property identifies $Q$ with $C$, and the branch assertions are vacuous. Repeating the argument for every geometric point gives every claimed fibre assertion.
